Title: HgTe Nanocrystal‐Gated Infrared Phototransistors With High Sensitivity, Extended Dynamic Range, and In‐Sensor Image Processing Capability

HgTe Nanocrystal-Gated Infrared Phototransistors With
High Sensitivity, Extended Dynamic Range, and In-Sensor
Image Processing Capability
Jingwen Wang, Binbin Wang, Xitian Yin, Qianxi Yang, Tao Luo, Hongkun Duan,
Shuren Zhou, Xinzheng Lan, Ying Wang,* and Zhiyong Zhang*
Mercury telluride (HgTe) nanocrystals (NCs) oﬀer adjustable absorption and
solution-processable fabrication, making them promising materials for low-
cost, high-resolution imaging across a wide infrared (IR) spectrum. However,
photodetectors based on HgTe NCs often suﬀer from high dark current,
elevated noise arising from trap states and interface defects, and limited
structural tunability, which constrain their sensitivity, dynamic range, and
applicability in intelligent vision applications. Here, it is reported a dual-gate
carbon nanotubes (CNTs) ﬁeld-eﬀect transistor incorporating an HgTe NC-
based PIN heterojunction as the top gate, which converts incident IR light into
a photovoltage that functions as a dynamic optical gate, while an independently
addressable local bottom gate adjusts the carrier concentration in the CNT
channel. This opto-electrically decoupled yet synergistic architecture enables
high responsivity (>103 A/W), excellent room-temperature speciﬁc detectivity
(1013 Jones) under low-power IR illumination, and a wide dynamic range of
170 dB to 1650 nm infrared irradiation when biased in the subthreshold region.
Furthermore, by leveraging gate-controllable and self-adaptive photoresponse,
it is demonstrated in-sensor convolutional processing and image fusion
at the device level. This dual-gate architecture provides a new pathway toward
high-performance IR photodetectors with in-sensor computing capabilities,
advancing their potential for next-generation machine vision systems.

range of applications, including semiconductor inspection,

have integrated HgTe NCs with hybrid conductive channels
such as organic semiconductors,[14] graphene,[15,16] or carbon
nanotubes (CNTs)[17] to facilitate charge separation or transport.
However, these systems often suﬀer from intrinsic trade-oﬀs
between IR absorption and gate modulation eﬃciency,[18] as well
as between gain and response speed,[19] due to photoelectric
conversion occurring within the same conducting medium.
Parallel to device exploration, signiﬁcant progress in material
synthesis and surface chemistry has driven performance im-
provements in HgTe NC photodetectors. For instance, precise
size control and ionic doping have extended spectral response up
to 18 μm,[20] while optimized ligand passivation have enhanced
electron mobility from ≈10−2 to 18.4 cm2 V−1 s−1.[21] Advanced
heterojunction architectures have further enabled broadband
IR detection, expanding spectral coverage and enhancing target
discrimination.[22] Additionally, improvements in defect pas-
sivation and interface engineering have led to state-of-the-art
performance metrics, including external quantum eﬃciencies
(EQEs) exceeding 40%, room-temperature detectivities around
on the order of 1011 Jones, and linear dynamic ranges of 90
≈120 dB.[23] Despite these advancements, HgTe NC devices
still fall short of established InGaAs and HgCdTe technolo-
gies, largely due to challenges such as inter-dot fusion, high
defect densities,[10,24], and low thermal budgets that limit post-
fabrication processing.[23] Moreover, the structural inﬂexibility of
conventional architectures hinders their integration into emerg-
ing in-sensor computing paradigms, which demand both high
performance and dynamic, electrically tunable functionality.
Overcoming these limitations calls for the development of novel
device platforms capable of oﬀering enhanced performance
and greater architectural adaptability—key to unlocking the full
potential of HgTe NCs in IR applications.
In this work, we present a HgTe NC-gated ﬁeld-eﬀect transis-
tor that employs an opto-electrical decoupling and synergy mech-
anism, integrating a PIN junction (akin to those found in photo-
voltaic IR detectors) with a CNT ﬁeld-eﬀect transistor (FET). The
Bi2S3/HgTe CQDs/Ag:HgTe heterojunction is deposited atop the
gate dielectric of the underlying FET, with CQDs spin-coated
onto sputtered n-type Bi2S3. This stratiﬁed conﬁguration ensures
well-deﬁned interfaces, overcoming issues common in binary or
blended CQD ﬁlms. The heterojunction eﬃciently absorbs inci-
dent IR light and generates an open-circuit voltage that serves
as a dynamic gate bias, modulating the work function of the
CNT channel and regulating the drain-source current. Leverag-
ing the FET’s internal gain and low ﬂicker noise, the device
achieves high responsivity (>103 A/W at 1650 nm), speciﬁc de-
tectivity of 1013 Jones under low-power IR illumination, and a
self-adaptive photoresponse enabling a broad dynamic range of
170 dB. The independently addressable local gate further facil-
itates programmable photocurrents and tunable output modes,
supporting in-sensor image processing.

2. Results and Discussion
2.1. Structure and Characterization of the HgTe NC-Gated
Phototransistor
The HgTe NC-gated phototransistor was developed based on
a PIN-structured photoresponsive unit. The HgTe CQDs were
synthesized using a previously reported continuous-dropwise
method,[25] which enables high critical nucleation concentra-
tion and precise control over nucleation and growth dynam-
ics. As shown in Figure 1a, the transmission electron mi-
croscopy (TEM) image reveals the branched morphology and
size distribution of the HgTe CQDs. The CQDs were assem-
bled into a 120 nm-thick active layer via solid-state, layer-by-layer
method, optimized to balance light absorption and junction de-
pletion. A hole-extracting layer was constructed using spheri-
cal Ag2Te CQDs (Figure 1b), which were sequentially treated
with HgCl2/methanol solution and 1,2-ethanedithiol (EDT) to
form a 20 nm-thick p-doped Ag:HgTe layer. Absorption spectra
in Figure 1c showed a sharp excitonic peak at 1650 nm for HgTe
CQD solids, while the Ag:HgTe ﬁlm exhibited broader absorp-
tion centered at 1700 nm. A 5 nm-thick n-type Bi2S3 thin ﬁlm
(work function: 4.22 eV) was integrated to enhance carrier sepa-
ration and facilitate eﬃcient photoelectron extraction.[26] The en-
ergy band alignment of each layer, derived from ultraviolet pho-
toelectron spectroscopy (see Figure S1, Supporting Information),
is illustrated in Figure 1d.
Upon IR irradiation, the HgTe CQD layer absorbs photons
and generates electron–hole pairs that are separated by the built-
in electric ﬁeld. Electrons accumulate in the Bi2S3 layer, while
holes migrate to the Ag:HgTe layer, resulting in a measurable
shift in the open-circuit voltage. To transduce this photovoltage
into an electrical signal, a CNT-based FET was integrated be-
neath the heterojunction, as illustrated in Figure 2a (with the
cross-sectional view of the device and the corresponding elec-
trical circuit provided in Figure S2, Supporting Information).
Polymer-sorted, solution-derived CNTs (>99.99% semiconduct-
ing purity) were deposited onto a 10 nm HfO2 gate dielectric in a
local-gate conﬁguration, forming a randomly oriented ﬁlm with
a tube density of 30 ≈35 CNTs/μm. Photolithography was used
to pattern the CNT ﬁlm and deﬁne the source/drain contacts
(Pd/Au, 30/40 nm). These contact electrodes were then passi-
vated with an HfO2 dielectric layer to restrict lateral charge trans-
port in the overlying CQD layer. A 6 nm Y2O3 ﬁlm (dielectric
constant: 𝜅≈8[27]) was deposited over the entire CNT channel,
acting as a high-𝜅photoelectric coupling layer that converts the
photovoltage into drain-source current modulation via electro-
static gating. Notably, Y2O3 can be directly deposited onto CNT

tating eﬃcient p-type conduction. Based on this, a p-on-n stacked
heterojunction was adopted, in which Bi2S3 was selectively pat-
terned on the Y2O3 ﬁlm using photolithography followed by a
lift-oﬀprocess, thereby deﬁning the eﬀective p-n junction region
within the FET channel. Photoexcited electrons accumulate in
the Bi2S3 layer, leading to an increase in hole density within the
CNT channel and, consequently, a measurable enhancement in
the drain–source current. Importantly, the selective patterning of
the Bi2S3 layer allows precise spatial deﬁnition of the photoac-
tive region without the need for direct patterning of the CQD
layers. This architecture eﬀectively decouples IR absorption and
carrier separation (within the PIN junction) from charge trans-
port (in the CNT channel), thereby reducing noise and suppress-
ing recombination losses while enabling synergistic device oper-
ation. In addition, the high-𝜅gate dielectric facilitates eﬃcient
photovoltage-induced gating, contributing to cooperative signal
ampliﬁcation.[29] Figure 2b shows the fabricated HgTe NC-gated
phototransistors with a channel length of 10 μm and width of
6 μm. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image and Raman
spectroscopy reveal the CNT ﬁlm morphology and a high G/D
band ratio of 21, indicating a low level of structural defects.
2.2. Photoresponse Characteristics
To evaluate the performance of HgTe NC-gated phototransistors,
we employed an electro-optical measurement setup with colli-
mated and modulated light. The output power was calibrated us-
ing a germanium power meter and an InGaAs photodiode, while
the beam spot size and intensity proﬁle were measured with a
standard InGaAs camera (see the calibrated incident light inten-
sity in Table S1, Supporting Information). Figure 2c shows the
transient photoresponse of the device under 1650 nm IR irra-
diation, with incident power density (Plight ) ranging from 0 to
11.1 W cm−2 at bias voltages of VDS = −0.1 V and VLG = 0 V.
A low VDS was selected to eﬀectively suppress dark current and
noise (see output characteristics and bottom-gate transfer curve
with gate leakage current in Figure S3, Supporting Information).
At low incident power density of 37.6 nW cm−2, a photocurrent
of 55.2 pA was measured, against a background current of 1.4
nA. The photocurrent is attributed to the HgTe heterojunction,
as conﬁrmed by comparing the photoresponse characteristics
of the device before and after PN junction deposition (Figure
S4, Supporting Information). As Plight increases, the photocur-
rent rises monotonically without noticeable saturation, even at
11.1 W cm−2. Figure 2d shows the extracted photocurrent versus
light power density curve, which exhibits a near-linear relation-
ship at low Plight and transitions to a logarithmic dependence at
higher Plight .

circuit voltage (Voc) and Plight is given by:

Figure 2d further demonstrates that the device exhibits high re-

channel. Notably, this high responsivity at low incident power is
attributed to a Voc-dominated gain mechanism enabled by elec-
trostatic gate coupling,[29] rather than the carrier trapping or trap-
dominated photogating eﬀects commonly observed in previously
reported phototransistors.[19,35,36]
2.3. Gate-Tunable Output Characteristic
The local gate electrode in the HgTe NC-gated phototransistor
enables modulation of the CNT channel’ local Fermi level, pro-
viding ﬂexible electrical control over both the photoresponse
and dark current. As shown in Figure 3a, the device’s dynamic
photocurrent was measured under weak 1650 nm irradiation
(Plight ranging from 37.6 nW cm−2 to 38.4 μW cm−2) at VDS =
−0.1 V across four typical VLGvalues. These correspond to oper-
ating points at near-minimum dark current, in the subthreshold
region, near turn-on, and in the linear region (Figure S5, Sup-
porting Information). As VLG increased, the photocurrent rose
from 55.2 pA at VLG = 0 V to 399.6 pA at VLG = −0.8 V un-
der low light (Plight = 37.6 nW cm−2). However, at VLG = −1.3 V,
no appreciable photoresponse was observed until Plight exceeded
0.8 μW cm−2, due to elevated dark current and associated noise.
Under a higher illumination (Plight = 38.4 μW cm−2), the pho-
tocurrent increased from 0.7 nA at VLG = 0 V to 5.9 nA at VLG
= −1.3 V, demonstrating the gate-tunable responsivity of the de-
vice. Figure 3b shows that for VLG values between 0 to −0.8 V
and under low irradiance, the photocurrent exhibits a near-linear
dependence on power density. In contrast, at VLG = −1.3 V,
the response follows a logarithmic trend—ﬁtted by the green
dotted line—indicative of the CNT FET operating in the linear
regime.

2.4. In-Sensor Convolution Processing and Image Fusion
The overall speed and power eﬃciency of traditional IR im-
age sensors are often limited by slow ADC conversion, as
well as redundant data transmission and processing. More-
over, their limited dynamic range frequently necessitates mul-
tiple imagers to simultaneously capture both bright and
dark details within a scene.[52,53] In contrast, HgTe NC-
gated phototransistors—featuring gate-tunable photoresponse
and self-adaptive behavior—enable partial in-sensor processing,
facilitating more eﬃcient computation, reduced data traﬃc, and
enhanced dynamic range perception. As shown in Figure 5a, we
present a conﬁguration for in-sensor convolutional processing
using 3 × 3 kernels to enhance features in night-vision images.
Analogue multiplication between the incident light intensity and
the gate-tunable photoresponse occurs directly at each detector
element, while current summation is achieved through intercon-
nects based on Kirchhoﬀ’s current law. A linear relationship be-
tween photocurrent and light intensity is adopted for weak-light
detection (see Methods: “Image Processing Implementation”).
Figure 5b shows both the original and processed images of scenes
containing architectural structures, pedestrians, and a wolf. The
processed outputs exhibit enhanced sharpness and improved fea-
ture clarity, enabling superior information extraction compared
to the raw input.
Figure 5c illustrates image fusion processing that leverages the
sensor’s self-adaptive photoresponse. Based on the distinct out-
put photocurrents at low and high intensities (Figure 2d), we set
a threshold of 1 nA (pixel value of 150) and acquired two images:
one reﬂecting the near-linear response regime (Figure 5c(i)) and
the other reﬂecting the logarithmic regime (Figure 5c(ii)). These
were fused using the following weighted expression: I (x, y) =
𝛼I1(x,y) + (1 −𝛼)I2(x,y), where I(x, y), I1(x,y), and I2(x,y) denote
the pixel values at coordinate (x, y) in the fused image and the
two individual mode outputs, respectively. The weighting factor
𝛼ranges from 0 to 1 and was set to 0.5 in this study. The re-
sulting image, shown in Figure 5c(iii), reveals additional details
(highlighted by the red dotted lines), demonstrating the detec-
tor’s ability to emulate the complementary functions of cone and
rod cells under complex lighting conditions.
3. Conclusion
In summary, we report a dual-gate HgTe NC-gated IR ﬁeld-eﬀect
transistor that synergistically integrates a PIN heterojunction
with a CNT FET, eﬀectively addressing key limitations of current
HgTe NC-based detectors—namely, high noise and restricted dy-
namic range. By decoupling optical absorption and carrier sepa-
ration (via the Bi2S3/HgTe/Ag:HgTe stack) from electrical mod-
ulation (via the CNT channel), the device achieves exceptional
performance, including a responsivity (>103 A/W), a peak spe-
ciﬁc detectivity of 1013 Jones, and a dynamic range of 170 dB.
This architecture further imparts adaptive light-response behav-
ior analogous to biological vision, while the independently ad-
dressable local gate enables tunable photoresponse modes. More-
over, we demonstrate in-sensor convolutional processing and im-
age fusion by leveraging locally gate-programmable photocur-
rents, which enhance target detection and dynamic range without
requiring backend computation. Future research should focus
on optimizing interconnects, control electronics, and monolithic
integration with silicon ROICs to accelerate the development of
compact, energy-eﬃcient machine vision systems.
4. Experimental Section
Synthesis of HgTe Nanocrystals:
To prepare a 1 m tri-n-octylphosphine
telluride (TOPTe) stock solution (used as a Te Precursor), 1.276 g of Te
shots were added to 10 mL of tri-n-octylphosphine (TOP) in a 20 mL glass
vial and heated at 160 °C for 2 h forming a yellowish, clear solution. Sepa-
rately, 4 mL of pre-degassed oleylamine (OLA) was added to a 20 mL glass
vial, followed by 0.3 mmol of HgCl2. The mixture was heated to 120 °C un-
der a nitrogen atmosphere and maintained for 30 min to ensure complete
dissolution of HgCl2. A precursor solution containing 200 μL of TOPTe di-
luted in 800 μL of OLA was then introduced into the HgCl2 solution at a
controlled rate of 0.2 mL·min−1 over 5 min using a syringe pump. After
an additional 2-min reaction, the mixture was quenched by adding 10 mL
of octane (OCT) containing 1 mmol of mercaptopropionic acid (MPA)
and allowed to cool naturally to room temperature. The resulting HgTe
nanocrystals were precipitated using isopropanol (IPA) and redispersed
in OCT.
Synthesis of Ag2Te CQDs:
In a 20 mL glass vial, 0.2 mmol of AgNO3
was dissolved in 5 mL of pre-degassed OLA and 0.5 mL of oleic acid (OA).
The mixture was heated to 70 °C under nitrogen and maintained for 30 min
to ensure complete dissolution. Subsequently, 0.5 mL of TOP was injected,
and the temperature was raised to 160 °C for 30 min, resulting in a trans-
parent orange precursor solution. Then, 100 μL of TOPTe was rapidly in-
jected, and the reaction proceeded for 10 min before being quenched with
10 mL of anhydrous tetrachloroethylene (TCE). After cooling to room tem-
perature, the Ag2Te CQDs were precipitated using IPA and redispersed in
OCT.

CNT ﬁlm is shown in Figure 2b.
Fabrication of HgTe NC-Gated Phototransistors:
Phototransistors were
fabricated on a Si/SiO2 substrate. First, local gate electrodes were pat-
terned via photolithography, followed by EBE deposition of 1/25 nm
Ti/Pd and a lift-oﬀprocess. A10 nm-thick HfO2 dielectric layer was de-
posited using atomic layer deposition (ALD). Contact vias were deﬁned
by photolithography and reactive ion etching (RIE). The CNT ﬁlm was
deposited as described above, and channels were patterned by selective
CNT removal using RIE. Source/drain contacts and passivation layers were
formed via photolithography, EBE deposition of 30/40 nm Pd/Au, ALD of
10 nm HfO2, and a lift-oﬀprocess. A 6 nm high-𝜅Y2O3 layer was pre-
pared by depositing 3 nm Y ﬁlm and thermal oxidizing it at 270 °C in air
for 10 min. The electron-extracting Bi2S3 layer (5 nm) was deposited on
Y2O3 via photolithography and magnetron sputtering. The HgTe NC active
layer (≈120 nm) was deposited using a layer-by-layer method involving: 1)
Drop-casting and spin-coating (2500 rpm, 30 s) of 50 mg mL−1 HgTe solu-
tion; 2) Ligand exchange in 0.01 m HgCl2/methanol (MeOH) solution for
10 s, followed by MeOH rinses; 3) Surface treatment using an EDT/HCl/
IPA solution (v/v/v = 1:5:5000) for 30 s. This cycle was repeated for 3–4
times. Finally, a 20 nm p-type Ag:HgTe layer was formed using solid-state
cation exchange by spin-coating 10 mg mL−1 Ag2Te CQDs, followed by the
same ligand exchange steps as above.
Characterization and Measurement:
Optical absorption spectra of
HgTe and Ag:HgTe CQD ﬁlms were measured in transmission mode us-
ing a Thermo Nexus 670 FTIR spectrometer. TEM and SEM imaging were
performed using a Talos F200X (Thermo Scientiﬁc, 200 kV) and FEI ZEISS
Sigma 300, respectively. CNT density was analyzed with NMMeasure soft-
ware. Raman spectra were collected using a LabRAM HR800 spectrometer
(Jobin-Yvon). Optoelectronic measurements used a supercontinuum laser
(NKT, 640–2100 nm), paired with a monochromator (IHR320) and power
attenuator (Thorlabs, NIR Ø25 mm). Beam proﬁles were characterized
using an InGaAs camera (First Light Vision C-Red3). Electrical measure-
ments were performed with a Keithley 4200 semiconductor analyzer un-
der ambient conditions. Noise spectra were measured using a PDA FS380
system, and response times were determined with an Agilent DSO7054A
oscilloscope.

tionship: In = ∑N
n=1 Pm ⋅Rmn, where VLG was biased in the subthreshold
region to enable enhanced sensitivity for weak-light detection, relevant to
night vision applications. In this expression, Rmndenotes the photorespon-
sivity matrix, Pm is the vector of incident light intensities, and In is the re-

image and performing the optoelectronic convolution operation, a matrix
of accumulated photocurrents was generated to construct the processed
image directly within the sensors.
To emulate image fusion analogous to biological vision, a threshold was
deﬁned—either based on photocurrent magnitude or the corresponding
grayscale value. Pixels above this threshold were ﬁltered out to extract a
low-light image, wherein a linear mapping between light intensity and pho-
tocurrent was applied, reﬂecting the device’s linear response under weak
illumination. Conversely, a high-light image was obtained by ﬁltering out
pixels below the threshold and applying a logarithmic mapping, consis-
tent with the sensor’s compressive response under strong illumination.
The ﬁnal fused image was generated by combining the two outputs using
a weighting factor to balance their contributions.
